ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Nephrology Referral — Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit for swelling of the face and legs and dark urine after a sore throat: urgent kidney and streptococcal tests, treatment of fluid overload and the infection, and an urgent nephrology referral

text.paragraph: Acute nephritic syndrome in a 28-year-old composer and pianist: swelling of the face and legs, cola-colored urine, blood pressure 162/100, and creatinine 1.62 mg/dL, two to three weeks after a febrile sore throat, with aching knees and ankles. Please confirm the cause, advise whether a kidney biopsy is needed, and guide fluid and blood pressure management and follow-up. [S]

list.item: Is this post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, or does anything point to another glomerular disease?
Does he need a kidney biopsy now, and what would make one necessary later?
Can he be managed as an outpatient, and how should fluid and blood pressure be treated?
Do his joint pains after the streptococcal infection mean acute rheumatic fever, and does he need an echocardiogram or penicillin prophylaxis?
How should he be monitored, and for how long, and what is the outlook for his kidneys?

text.paragraph: A febrile sore throat two to three weeks ago, untreated. About ten days later aching knees and ankles without joint swelling, three days of crampy abdominal pain and vomiting, and a low fever; then four days of puffy eyelids in the mornings, swollen ankles, less urine that looks like cola, and a mild headache. He took ibuprofen 400 mg two or three times a day for five days; stopped today. No rash, cough with blood, sinus symptoms, or previous kidney disease known to him. No family history of kidney disease is recorded. Examination today: blood pressure 162/100, pulse 88, temperature 37.6 °C, weight 64.2 kg against a usual 61 kg; periorbital and 2+ ankle edema; mildly red throat without exudate; lungs clear; no murmur; joints without effusion; no purpura. Rapid antigen test for group A streptococcus positive. Urgent results today: creatinine 1.62 mg/dL (eGFR 59), BUN 31 mg/dL, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, albumin 3.6 g/dL; hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, white cells 8.9 and platelets 265 thousand per microliter; CRP 18 mg/L and ESR 38 mm/h; C3 42 mg/dL (low) and C4 24 mg/dL (normal); ASO 620 and anti-DNase B 980 IU/mL; urine red cells 60 per high-power field with red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells; urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 1400 mg/g. Started today: penicillin V 500 mg twice a day for ten days, furosemide 40 mg each morning, sodium below 2 g a day, about 1.5 liters of fluid a day, and daily weights [S]

list.item: He is afraid his kidneys will be damaged for good. [S]
He loses income for every concert and lesson he misses. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg on January 27, 1756, the son of Leopold Mozart, a musician in the service of the Archbishop of Salzburg. Of the seven children of his parents' marriage only two survived: his sister Maria Anna, born July 30, 1751, and Wolfgang. [D]
In Vienna in late 1762, on the family's second journey, an attack of scarlet fever kept him in bed for a fortnight. [D]

At The Hague in the autumn of 1765, after his sister's dangerous illness, he was seized with a violent attack of fever that reduced him to extreme weakness for several weeks; he kept writing on a board laid across his bed. [D]

In 1767 the family fled a smallpox outbreak in Vienna to Olmütz, but he and then his sister caught smallpox there; the family was taken in by Count Leopold Anton von Podstatzky, Dean of Olmütz, and his illness was so severe that he lay blind for nine days and had to protect his eyes for several weeks afterwards. [D]
In the spring of 1783 he fell ill with an illness his biographer calls cholera, during an epidemic in Vienna. [D]

In a letter to his daughter dated September 14, 1784, Leopold Mozart wrote that his son had been very ill in Vienna: he had become overheated at Paisiello's new opera and had gone out into the open air to find the servant who had his overcoat, and this "brought on rheumatic fever, which without careful attention might have turned to typhus." He quoted his son's letter: "I have had raging colic every day for a fortnight at the same hour, accompanied by violent vomiting," and that his doctor, Sigmund Barisani, visited him almost daily. [D]
In 1784, up to the time of the episode, he lived at Graben 29 in Vienna. [D]
His mother died in Paris on July 3, 1778, while traveling with him, after an illness of some weeks during which she was bled; the cause is not recorded in the cited source. [D]
One author argues that he had frequent attacks of tonsillitis throughout his life and that in 1784 he developed a post-streptococcal Schönlein-Henoch syndrome. [R]

list.item: Composer and pianist; self-employed, with income from his own subscription concerts, teaching piano pupils, and commissions; moved to this city from his home town about three years ago [S]
Married; lives with his wife in a rented city-center apartment and is due to move to a larger one at the end of the month [S]
Works late into the night and performs several evenings a week, often in crowded halls; enjoys billiards and dancing [S]
Alcohol: wine or punch with friends on two or three evenings a week, two drinks at most (AUDIT-C 2); never used tobacco; no other drugs [S]
Took ibuprofen 400 mg two or three times a day for five days for the aching joints, before this visit; no other medicines or supplements [S]
Health insurance through a performing artists' plan; worried about missing concerts and lessons, which he is paid for only when he plays or teaches [S]

list.item: Swelling of the face and legs with cola-colored urine, less urine, raised blood pressure, and reduced kidney function (acute nephritic picture), two to three weeks after a febrile sore throat and followed by aching knees and ankles, crampy abdominal pain, and vomiting; cause not yet confirmed at intake; urgent nephrology consultation requested: active, confirmed [S]
Group A streptococcal pharyngitis, rapid antigen test positive at intake with a mildly red throat two to three weeks after the sore throat began; penicillin V started: active, confirmed [S]

Sodium below 2 g a day, fluids limited to about 1.5 liters a day while swollen, and daily morning weights, with a call if weight rises 1 kg in a day, urine output falls, or headache, vision change, or breathlessness appear. Guideline: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases (Kidney Int 2021;100(4S):S1-S276) (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, chronic kidney disease and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

Furosemide each morning for edema and hypertension until he is back to his usual weight with normal blood pressure, with potassium and creatinine checked at each visit. Guideline: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases (Kidney Int 2021;100(4S):S1-S276) (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, chronic kidney disease and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

Penicillin V for ten days to eradicate group A streptococcus. Guideline: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases (Kidney Int 2021;100(4S):S1-S276) (2021); Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis: 2012 Update (Shulman ST, et al. Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102) (2012) [S]

Stop ibuprofen and avoid all NSAIDs while the kidneys recover; acetaminophen for pain. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, chronic kidney disease and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]
